questions.stem: Water is found entering a small vessel. What does the Transport Canada procedure say to do first?
options: Abandon ship at once
Find the leak before doing anything else, even if the water is rising
Call out where the water is, then start the pumps or bail
Fill out the incident report
questions.explanation: The procedure starts with calling out the location of the water ('Water in or on the ...') and starting the pumps or bailing, then finding where the water enters. Abandoning at once is for when stability is threatened, and the incident report comes last.

questions.stem: Which sequence matches the Transport Canada taking-on-water procedure?
options: Notify authorities, abandon ship, find the entry, then pump
Call out location, pump or bail, find the entry, notify if at risk, stop or slow the leak, prepare to abandon if stability is threatened
Prepare to abandon, call out location, stop the leak, then start pumping
Find the entry, file the incident report, then call out the location
questions.explanation: The order is call out, pump or bail, find the entry, notify if the vessel is at risk, stop or slow the leak (or consider grounding), prepare to abandon if stability is threatened, keep authorities informed, then complete the incident report.

questions.stem: A moving vessel has a leak below the waterline. Why does the BOATsmart! guidance say to stop her completely?
options: It reduces the water pressure on the hull and slows the inflow
It lets the propeller cool down
It makes the hole larger so it can be found
It stops water entering through the seacocks
questions.explanation: The guidance says stopping a moving craft reduces the water pressure on the hull and slows the inflow. It has nothing to do with the propeller or with enlarging the hole.

questions.stem: A raw-water hose has burst in the engine space. What is the quickest way to stop the flow?
options: Open all the hatches
Increase engine speed
Switch off the compass light
Close its seacock
questions.explanation: Closing the seacock of the burst hose stops the sea from coming in. The other actions do nothing to the leak, which is why seacocks must be accessible and work by hand.

questions.stem: Which of these are suitable ways to stop a small leak in a hull according to the BOATsmart! guidance?
options: Water-soluble glue
A tow line wrapped round the hull amidships
Tapered wooden plugs, a hull patch kit, or towels and rags pressed into the hole
Ice packed into the hole
questions.explanation: The guidance lists tapered wooden plugs, a patch kit, and towels, rags or other malleable material, and says to carry them as a standing kit. The other options do not make a watertight seal.

questions.stem: Why does water sloshing about inside a flooded compartment endanger the vessel beyond its weight?
options: It raises the centre of buoyancy above the deck
It is a free surface that moves to the low side and reduces stability
It increases the vessel's metacentric height
It changes the magnetic compass reading
questions.explanation: Water moving inside the hull is a free surface: it flows to the low side as the vessel heels and cuts the righting effect. It reduces, not increases, GM, and does not affect the compass.

questions.stem: Flooding cannot be controlled and the nearest shoreline is a gravel beach with a light swell on one side and a rocky headland with heavy surf on the other. What does the guidance support?
options: Deliberately beaching her on the gravel beach, avoiding the rocks and surf
Running onto the rocky headland where she will be easiest to find
Staying in deep water to avoid damage to the hull
Anchoring in mid-channel and waiting
questions.explanation: The template says to consider grounding the vessel if the flooding cannot be controlled, and Boating Magazine says grounding on a bar or beach may beat sinking as long as you avoid jagged rocks and high surf.

questions.stem: The master decides the vessel may sink. Which set of actions matches the guidance?
options: Lifejackets stowed to avoid snagging, a PAN PAN, and wait for the water to stop
Only the crew put on lifejackets, then a MAYDAY without a position
All passengers go below to stay dry while the crew bail
Lifejackets on and everyone accounted for, a MAYDAY with position, persons on board and nature of distress, and preparation to abandon
questions.explanation: BOATsmart! and Boating Magazine advise lifejackets for everyone and a check that everyone is present, and a MAYDAY on channel 16 with location, number of people and nature of the distress. The template adds preparing to abandon if stability is threatened.

questions.stem: Which statement about SVR s. 602 is correct?
options: Only passenger vessels need seacocks
Wet exhausts must have a seacock like everything else
Every vessel must be able to positively shut off underwater penetrations, with wet exhaust systems excepted
Seacocks are required only on vessels over 12 m
questions.explanation: Section 602(1) requires the means for positively shutting off underwater penetrations on every vessel, except wet exhaust systems. It is not limited to passenger vessels or to length.

questions.stem: What pumping equipment must a 7 m passenger-carrying vessel under SVR Part 4 carry?
options: A manual bilge pump only
A bailer or a manual bilge pump
A powered bilge pump with an alarm
None, since she is under 9 m
questions.explanation: Section 412 requires a bailer or manual bilge pump for vessels up to 9 m (and a manual bilge pump over 9 m). The bailer or pump can be omitted only if the vessel cannot retain enough water to capsize or its compartments are sealed.

questions.stem: A tug strikes a log and sustains damage that affects her seaworthiness. She does not sink, no one is hurt, and she returns to port. Is there a TSB reporting duty?
options: Yes: damage that affects seaworthiness or renders the ship unfit for its purpose is reportable, with the available facts as soon as possible and the rest within 30 days
No, because she did not sink
No, because no one was injured
Yes, but only if the damage costs more than a set amount
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(d)(vi) lists damage that affects seaworthiness or renders the ship unfit for its purpose, whether or not she sinks and whether or not anyone is hurt. There is no cost threshold in that paragraph.
